title: Definition of consumer
summary: A 'consumer' is a person who buys goods or hires/avails services for a price (paid, promised or partly paid). It includes online and teleshopping purchases. It excludes people who buy goods for resale or for a commercial purpose.

title: Definition of defect
summary: A 'defect' means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard of goods that the law, a contract or the seller's claim requires.

title: Definition of deficiency
summary: A 'deficiency' means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature or manner of a service that the law or a contract requires, including negligence by the service provider that causes loss to the consumer.

title: Unfair trade practice
summary: 'Unfair trade practice' covers misleading or deceptive practices by a seller or service provider. It includes refusing to take back defective goods or withdraw deficient services and refund the price within the stipulated period (or within 30 days if no period is stated).

title: Jurisdiction of District Commission
summary: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission hears complaints up to a set value of goods/services paid. The pecuniary limit was revised by rules in 2021 (commonly stated as up to Rs 50 lakh — verify current limit). A complaint can be filed where the opposite party lives or works, or where the complainant lives or works.

title: Manner of filing a complaint
summary: A consumer can file a complaint with the District Commission about goods sold or services provided. Complaints may be filed electronically (for example through the e-Daakhil portal).

title: Reliefs the District Commission can order
summary: If the complaint is proved, the District Commission can order things such as removing the defect, replacing the goods, refunding the price, paying compensation for loss or injury, and stopping the unfair trade practice.

title: Limitation period for complaints
summary: A consumer complaint should generally be filed within two years from the date the cause of action arose. The Commission may admit a late complaint if sufficient cause for the delay is shown.

title: Filing fee for consumer complaints
summary: Filing fees depend on the value of the claim. Small claims (commonly stated as up to Rs 5 lakh) are understood to carry no filing fee. Always confirm the current fee on the e-Daakhil portal before filing.

act: National Consumer Helpline (Dept. of Consumer Affairs)
title: National Consumer Helpline
summary: The National Consumer Helpline (toll-free 1915) and its online portal/app let consumers register grievances against companies before going to a Consumer Commission. It is free and often resolves refund disputes without litigation.

title: Online filing of consumer complaints
summary: e-Daakhil is the government portal for filing consumer complaints online, paying fees and tracking cases, without needing a lawyer.

title: Compensation for breach of contract
summary: When a contract is broken, the party who suffers can claim compensation for loss or damage that naturally arose from the breach, or that both parties knew was likely when they made the contract. Remote or indirect losses are not covered.

title: Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property
summary: A person who is dispossessed of immovable property without consent and other than by due process of law can sue to recover possession. Such a suit must be filed within six months of dispossession.

title: Time limit for civil money claims
summary: Most civil suits to recover money under a contract (for example a deposit or unpaid dues) must be filed within three years, usually counted from when the payment was due or the contract was broken. The exact starting point depends on the specific Article that applies — a lawyer should confirm.

title: Status of the Model Tenancy Act
summary: The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 is a model law issued by the Central Government. It applies only in states/UTs that have enacted their own law based on it. In other states, the state's own rent control law and the rent agreement govern the tenancy.

title: Security deposit
summary: Under the model law, the security deposit for residential premises cannot exceed two months' rent (six months for non-residential), and must be refunded when the landlord takes back vacant possession, after lawful deductions owed by the tenant.

title: Rent agreement terms on deposit
summary: Where no specific state law applies, the refund of a security deposit is governed by the rent agreement. Deductions are generally limited to unpaid rent, unpaid bills, and actual damage beyond normal wear and tear, and the landlord should be able to show them.

title: Status of the labour codes
summary: The Code on Wages, 2019 consolidates older wage laws (including the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 and the Minimum Wages Act, 1948). The labour codes were brought into force by government notification (reported effective 21 November 2025 — verify, and check state rules).

title: Time limit for payment of wages
summary: Wages must be paid on time: monthly wages before the 7th day of the following month (with shorter limits for daily, weekly and fortnightly wages). When an employee is removed, dismissed, retrenched or resigns, wages due must be paid within two working days.

title: Claims under the Code
summary: An employee can file a claim for unpaid wages or other dues under the Code before the authority appointed by the government. Claims generally must be filed within three years.

title: Where to complain about unpaid salary
summary: Unpaid salary complaints usually go to the office of the Labour Commissioner/authority of the state where the employee worked. Senior or managerial employees may need to file a civil suit or send a legal notice instead, because some labour laws cover only certain categories of employees.

title: Cheating
summary: Cheating — deceiving someone dishonestly to deliver property or do something they would not otherwise do — is an offence. This section replaced Section 420 of the IPC from 1 July 2024.

title: Criminal breach of trust
summary: Dishonestly misusing or keeping property that was entrusted to you is criminal breach of trust. This replaced Section 406 of the IPC.

title: Criminal intimidation
summary: Threatening someone with injury to their person, reputation or property to cause alarm or force them to act is criminal intimidation.

title: Dishonour of cheque
summary: If a cheque issued to pay a debt bounces for insufficient funds, it can be an offence after a demand notice is sent and payment is not made within the time allowed. These cases have strict timelines and should be handled with a lawyer.

title: Who can get free legal aid
summary: Free legal services are available to groups including women, children, SC/ST members, industrial workmen, people with disabilities, victims of disasters or trafficking, people in custody, and people below a notified income limit. Legal aid is provided through District/State Legal Services Authorities (NALSA helpline 15100).

act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
title: Right to reside in shared household
summary: A woman in a domestic relationship has the right to reside in the shared household, whether or not she has any title or ownership in it, and cannot be evicted except by procedure established by law.

title: Emergency and help numbers
summary: Emergency (police/ambulance/fire): 112. Women's helpline: 181. National Consumer Helpline: 1915. NALSA free legal aid: 15100.

title: New criminal laws from 1 July 2024
summary: From 1 July 2024 the Indian Penal Code, 1860 was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. Offences committed before that date may still be dealt with under the old laws.

title: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 replaced
summary: The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 was replaced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (in force from July 2020).
